sections.title: Framing the history by abnormal cell line

blocks.text: Most blood disorders present as **too many or too few cells of one lineage** (red cells, white cells or platelets), as abnormal bleeding or clotting, or as enlarged nodes or spleen. Take a complete general history first, then ask questions aimed at the count that is abnormal. Symptoms are often vague (tiredness, malaise), and anaemia and the chronic leukaemias are usually picked up on a routine blood test rather than at the bedside.

blocks.title: Targeted questions for each abnormal count
rows: Breathlessness, fatigue, chest pain; are white cells low too; is it new or long-standing; diet
Severe anaemia can worsen ischaemic heart disease; low counts in two lines suggest marrow failure; diet points to haematinic lack
Headache, blurred vision, itch; smoking, lung disease, dehydration; high WCC (basophils)
Separates primary polycythaemia (check JAK2) from secondary or relative causes
Recent infection; asthma, eczema or other allergy
Neutrophilia is usually reactive; allergy raises eosinophils; ask for a film, because immature cells suggest malignancy
Recent infection, mouth ulcers, family history, full drug history
Infection may be cause or effect; drugs are a frequent cause; benign neutropenia occurs in young women
Headache, itch, bleeding; features of infection or cancer; burning red feet
Reactive thrombocytosis is commoner than primary; very high counts can paradoxically cause bleeding
Bleeding, recent viral illness, rheumatological disease, drugs, past operations, labour, dental extractions
Immune thrombocytopenia may follow a viral illness, mainly in children (see pitfall)

blocks.title: Anaemia: symptoms and how severe it is
items: Non-specific: tiredness, weakness, breathlessness, headache, palpitations, light-headedness or postural dizziness.
It can **unmask or worsen** angina, claudication or heart failure.
Grade severity by the effort that brings on breathlessness (walking on the flat, one flight of stairs).

**Speed of onset matters**: sudden loss (e.g. bleeding) gives worse symptoms than slowly developing anaemia, which may be silent because of circulatory compensation and a rise in 2,3-BPG that shifts the oxygen dissociation curve to the right.
Pica (craving non-food items such as dirt) and hair loss hint at iron deficiency.

blocks.title: Looking for the cause of anaemia
items: **Iron deficiency** is usually from GI loss or heavy periods: ask about melaena, haematemesis, rectal bleeding, ulcers or colitis, bowel surgery, NSAIDs or anticoagulants; in women ask how long periods last, clots and how many pads or tampons are used per day.
**Macrocytic anaemia**: alcohol intake, a vegan diet (B12), previous gastrectomy (no intrinsic factor) or terminal ileal resection (B12 not absorbed).
**Chronic disease** (normocytic): rheumatoid arthritis, infective endocarditis, CKD (partly from reduced erythropoietin).
**Travel and residence**: in many regions chronic malaria or gut parasites are the cause.

**Ethnicity and family**: thalassaemia (Mediterranean, southern Asian), sickle cell disease (African), hereditary spherocytosis; pernicious anaemia clusters in families without a clear Mendelian pattern.

blocks.text: Red cell shape gives history clues: **oval macrocytes** suggest B12 or folate deficiency, **round macrocytes** suggest alcohol or liver disease, and recent bleeding raises the MCV because young red cells are large.

blocks.title: Polycythaemia and thrombocythaemia
items: Investigate a haematocrit that stays **above 0.52 in men or 0.48 in women for more than 2 months**; values above 0.60 (men) or 0.56 (women) can be taken as true (absolute) erythrocytosis.
**Polycythaemia vera** often creeps up in people over 60: fatigue, itch (classically after a hot bath), vertigo, headache, visual upset, or a thrombosis or bleed. JAK2 V617F is present in over 90%.
PV also brings arterial thrombosis (especially stroke), venous thrombosis, hepatosplenomegaly and gout.
**Secondary causes**: smoking and chronic lung disease (hypoxia). **Relative (Gaisböck's) polycythaemia**: hypertension, smoking, alcohol excess and diuretics.
**Essential thrombocythaemia** may cause erythromelalgia: burning pain, redness and warmth of the extremities, mainly the feet.

blocks.text: Neutropenia is usually a count **below 1.5 × 10^9/L**, and below 0.5 × 10^9/L is critically low. Fever may be the only sign of infection, and sepsis with shock can follow within hours without IV antibiotics, so a neutropenic patient must know whom to call when febrile.
A vegan diet is short of **both iron and vitamin B12**, so ask about diet in any anaemia.

Kumar's history table links immune thrombocytopenia to a recent viral illness. That pattern belongs mainly to **children**; Davidson points out that in **adults** a preceding viral infection is unusual, and adult ITP is commoner in women and may come with connective tissue disease. Follow Davidson.

sections.title: Haemato-oncology history: symptoms, background and fitness

blocks.text: When a blood cancer is possible, organise the symptoms into three groups: **marrow failure**, **mass effect** of malignant tissue, and **systemic (constitutional)** features. Then cover risk factors, family history and the patient's **fitness for treatment**.

blocks.title: Three symptom groups in suspected haematological malignancy
rows: Anaemia (fatigue, breathlessness, poor exercise tolerance); low platelets (easy bruising, bleeding); low white cells (recurrent infection, mouth ulcers, fever)
Left upper abdominal discomfort, bloating, early satiety from gastric compression, back pain; splenic infarct gives severe pain spreading to the left shoulder tip, with a rub
Swellings in the neck, jaw, axilla or groin
Malaise, fevers, drenching night sweats (needing a change of nightclothes), itch, unintentional weight loss that should always be quantified

blocks.title: Lymph node and lymphoma history
items: How fast did it appear and grow? Is it painful? Reactive nodes grow quickly and hurt; nodes from blood cancers are usually **painless**.
Weight loss with drenching night sweats points to haematological malignancy, particularly lymphoma.
**Hodgkin lymphoma**: commonest presentation is a painless cervical node; also ask about itch and **pain at the node site after drinking alcohol**.

blocks.title: Myeloma and recurrent infection
items: **Myeloma (CRAB)**: symptoms of high calcium, renal impairment, anaemia, and bone pain or fractures; secondary amyloid may enlarge the tongue.
Recurrent infection such as pneumonia may be the **first sign** of leukaemia (neutropenia), myeloma, HIV (lymphopenia) or immunoglobulin deficiency.
Immunoglobulin deficiency gives recurrent sinusitis and chest infections and may lead to bronchiectasis.

blocks.title: Background history
rows: Blood disease or malignancy; ages and health of siblings
Siblings are potential allogeneic transplant donors

blocks.title: Drug history
items: Blood loss: aspirin and NSAIDs (patients often forget over-the-counter aspirin). Haemolysis: sulphonamides. Aplasia: chloramphenicol.

Neutropenia: carbimazole, propylthiouracil, captopril, phenytoin, carbamazepine, valproate, sulphonamides, penicillins, some antidepressants (amitriptyline, dosulepin, mianserin), dapsone, chloroquine.

blocks.title: Treatment history
items: Iron or B12 injections; regular transfusion (MDS, myelofibrosis, marrow failure); erythropoietin (CKD); venesection (polycythaemia, haemochromatosis).
Splenectomy; steroids or immunosuppression for ITP; immunoglobulin infusions; factor VIII or IX concentrate.
Chemotherapy, radiotherapy or marrow transplant for leukaemia, lymphoma or myeloma, and how these affected daily life.
Anticoagulants: drug, duration, INR monitoring and any bleeding problems.

blocks.text: **Fitness for treatment**: record comorbidities and social circumstances, and estimate **performance status** from activities of daily living (washing, dressing, shopping, cooking). Performance status predicts how well a patient will tolerate chemotherapy or stem cell transplantation.
Recurrent infection should always raise the possibility of an underlying acute or chronic blood disorder.

Some MCQ answer keys give mediastinal nodes as the commonest Hodgkin presentation. Davidson and Kumar both describe **painless, rubbery neck (or supraclavicular) nodes** as typical, with a mediastinal mass mainly in a subgroup (often young women). Follow Davidson.

A bleeding history answers three questions: is the defect **generalised** (several sites, spontaneous, or out of proportion to injury)? Is it **inherited or acquired**? Does the pattern suggest a **platelet/vascular** or a **coagulation** problem?

blocks.title: Bleeding checklist
items: **Site and duration** of bleeding, and age at first problem: severe inherited defects show in infancy (sometimes prolonged umbilical stump bleeding); mild ones surface later after surgery, childbirth, dental extraction or trauma, or on a pre-operative screen.
**Trigger**: spontaneous bleeding means a more severe defect than bleeding only after injury.

**Surgical challenges**: dental extraction, tonsillectomy and circumcision stress haemostasis. **Immediate** bleeding points to a platelet plug (primary haemostasis) defect; **delayed** bleeding to a coagulation defect.
**Family history** and **drugs** (antiplatelets, anticoagulants, fibrinolytics, herbal remedies).
**Other illness**, e.g. liver disease.

blocks.title: Platelet/VWF versus coagulation-factor bleeding
rows: Skin petechiae, mucosa: nose, gums, GI tract, menorrhagia, prolonged oozing from cuts
Joints (haemarthrosis), muscles, deep soft tissue, retroperitoneum, brain

blocks.title: Inherited bleeding disorders
items: **Haemophilia A** (factor VIII) and **B** (factor IX) are X-linked recessive. Severe forms bleed spontaneously into weight-bearing joints, especially knees, and big muscles (thigh, iliopsoas, calf); repeated haemarthroses lead to arthropathy.
**Von Willebrand disease** is autosomal dominant with incomplete penetrance. VWF (chromosome 12) tethers platelets to exposed collagen and protects factor VIII from breakdown.
Older patients treated with donor-derived factor VIII may have been exposed to hepatitis viruses and HIV; ask whether they know their status.

blocks.text: A negative family history does **not** rule out an inherited disorder: about **one-third of haemophilia** arises without one. Repeated bleeding from one site suggests a local structural lesion rather than a coagulopathy.
Routine coagulation screens miss some causes (e.g. von Willebrand disease, scurvy, certain anticoagulants). If the history is convincing but screens are normal, measure **VWF and platelet function**.

blocks.title: Thrombosis history: risk factors
items: Patient: obesity, older age, smoking, oral contraceptive or HRT, pregnancy, prolonged immobility or long-distance travel.
Surgical: lower-limb orthopaedic surgery, trauma, pelvic or abdominal surgery (especially for cancer).
Medical: malignancy, heart failure, vasculitis, inflammatory bowel disease.
Haematological: factor V Leiden, prothrombin gene mutation, antiphospholipid syndrome, protein C, protein S or antithrombin deficiency.
Haematological causes of **arterial** thrombosis: polycythaemia, sickle cell anaemia, heparin-induced thrombocytopenia with thrombosis, SLE, antiphospholipid syndrome, protein C or S deficiency.

blocks.text: Risk factors multiply: **factor V Leiden plus the oral contraceptive** raises thrombotic risk about 100-fold.

blocks.title: When to consider thrombophilia testing
items: Venous thrombosis before age 45, or recurrent venous thrombosis.
A first-degree relative with unprovoked or repeated clots.
Both arterial and venous clots in the same patient.
Unusual sites: cerebral veins, hepatic vein (Budd–Chiari), portal or mesenteric veins.

sections.title: Inspection: general, hands, face, mouth, skin, fundi and bones

blocks.title: Position and order
items: Patient lying flat on one pillow, as for the abdominal examination.

Order: general inspection → hands and pulse → epitrochlear and axillary nodes → face and mouth → cervical nodes from behind (sitting up) → bony tenderness → abdomen and inguinal nodes → legs → fundi, temperature chart and urinalysis.

blocks.title: General inspection
rows: Weight loss, a systemic feature of haematological malignancy

blocks.title: Signs of anaemia
items: Pallor of skin and mucous membranes (conjunctivae).
Tachycardia, tachypnoea, systolic flow murmur.
Raised JVP, ankle oedema, cardiac failure, postural hypotension.
Clues to cause: jaundice (haemolysis), bone deformity (thalassaemia), oedema, hypertension and excoriations (CKD).

blocks.text: Palmar crease pallor suggests Hb below about 70 g/L, but nail-bed and palmar pallor are **unreliable**. **Conjunctival pallor** is better: finding it helps, but its absence does not exclude anaemia.

blocks.title: Hands, face and mouth
rows: Leukaemic infiltration, especially acute monocytic leukaemia
Marrow failure (e.g. aplasia); ulceration also with neutropenia

blocks.text: The textbook iron-deficiency signs (spoon nails, angular stomatitis, papillary atrophy of the tongue, brittle hair and nails, and dysphagia with glossitis in Plummer–Vinson syndrome) are generally seen only when deficiency is **very long-standing**, so their absence does not exclude it.

blocks.title: Skin bleeding
items: **Petechiae**: pinpoint, flat, non-blanching bleeds into the dermis, typical of thrombocytopenia (Talley lists counts below 100 × 10^9/L) or platelet dysfunction.
**Ecchymoses**: bruises larger than 5 mm. **Purpura** covers both.
**Palpable (raised) purpura** is not from low platelets; think vasculitis or bacteraemia.
Henoch–Schönlein purpura: palpable purpura over buttocks and legs, with glomerulonephritis, arthralgia and abdominal pain.
Scurvy: perifollicular purpura on the legs is almost diagnostic.
Flank or peri-umbilical haematoma means retroperitoneal bleeding; always examine joints for haemarthrosis.

blocks.text: Spontaneous bleeding is unusual until platelets fall **below 20 × 10^9/L** (unless function is also impaired); below **10 × 10^9/L** retinal and intracranial haemorrhage become possible.

blocks.title: Fundi, bones, neurology and legs
items: **Fundi**: hyperviscosity (macroglobulinaemia, myeloproliferative disease, CML) or leucostasis gives engorged retinal veins, haemorrhage and later papilloedema; haemorrhages also occur with low platelets; yellow-white patches suggest toxoplasma or CMV.
**Bones**: with the patient sitting, tap the spine with a fist and press the sternum, clavicles and shoulders; tenderness suggests marrow expansion by myeloma, lymphoma or carcinoma.

**Neurology**: confusion or fluctuating consciousness (hyperviscosity); leg weakness or paraesthesia (cord compression in myeloma); B12 deficiency causes peripheral neuropathy and subacute combined degeneration (early loss of vibration and position sense), even without anaemia.

**Legs**: ulcers near the malleoli in haemolytic anaemias (sickle cell, hereditary spherocytosis), thalassaemia, macroglobulinaemia, TTP, polycythaemia and Felty's; signs of venous disease or current DVT; haemophilic arthropathy of weight-bearing joints.

blocks.text: The Hess (tourniquet) test is now of historical interest only: a cuff held 10 mmHg above diastolic for 5 minutes; fewer than 5 petechiae per cm² is normal, more than 20 suggests thrombocytopenia, a platelet function defect or capillary fragility.

blocks.note: Look at: head-to-toe signs with insets of koilonychia, glossitis and angular stomatitis, gum hypertrophy in AML, fundal haemorrhage, gangrenous toe in thrombocytosis and a haemophilic joint
Look at: flat, non-blanching pinpoint petechiae of thrombocytopenia or platelet dysfunction
Compare with Fig. 21.4: large ecchymoses versus thrombocytopenic petechiae
Look at: prominent, injected scleral vessels in polycythaemia vera
Look at: palpable purpura on the legs in Henoch–Schönlein purpura

blocks.title: Technique, group by group
items: **Epitrochlear**: flex the elbow to 90°, cup it in your hand and feel just above and in front of the medial epicondyle. An enlarged node is usually pathological (local infection, non-Hodgkin lymphoma, sarcoidosis, rarely syphilis).

**Axillary**: rest the patient's relaxed arm on your forearm and push your opposite hand high into the axilla. Feel all five groups: central, lateral, pectoral (medial), infraclavicular and subscapular.

**Cervical** (patient sitting, examiner behind): submental, submandibular, jugular chain, posterior triangle, occipital, postauricular, preauricular; then the **supraclavicular** fossae from the front with the shoulders shrugged.
**Inguinal**: a horizontal group along the inguinal ligament and a vertical group along the femoral vessels. **Para-aortic** nodes are rarely palpable; a deep central abdominal mass may be one.

blocks.title: Describing a node
rows: Localised (local infection, early lymphoma) or generalised (late lymphoma, systemic disease)
Over 1 cm is usually abnormal; record in cm
Hard: carcinoma; rubbery: lymphoma; soft: may be normal
Fixed nodes are more likely to be infiltrated by carcinoma
Always examine the region the node drains (e.g. teeth for neck nodes, breast for axilla)

blocks.title: Which findings predict serious disease (especially lymphoma)?
Localised nodes: where to look next
rows: Metastasis from chest, abdomen (stomach: Troisier's sign) or pelvis
Upper-limb infection, breast cancer, disseminated malignancy
Lower-limb infection, sexually transmitted infection, abdominal or pelvic cancer
Oropharyngeal and head and neck cancers; scalp, ear, teeth, thyroid

blocks.title: Generalised versus localised lymphadenopathy
rows: Lymphoma; leukaemia (CLL, ALL); EBV, CMV, HIV; TB, brucellosis, syphilis; toxoplasmosis; RA, SLE; sarcoidosis; phenytoin
Local acute or chronic infection; metastatic carcinoma; lymphoma, especially Hodgkin

blocks.text: First tests in lymphadenopathy are FBC, ESR and chest X-ray. Diagnosis of lymphoma needs **biopsy** of a representative node (excision, or core for deep disease); fine-needle aspiration is inadequate.

Exam keyword pairs: fever + sore throat + nodes (± rash after ampicillin) = infectious mononucleosis; fever + nodes + visual symptoms = toxoplasmosis; prolonged fever + nodes + hepatosplenomegaly = lymphoma.

Small cervical nodes are often palpable in healthy young adults, and small firm mobile inguinal nodes are common in thin normal people; judge size, consistency, fixation and context before calling them abnormal.

blocks.note: Look at: the eight cervical and supraclavicular node groups, with photographs of cervical and submandibular lymphadenopathy

sections.title: Spleen, liver and the rest of the abdomen

blocks.text: The normal spleen (about 11 cm long) lies under the ribs and **cannot be felt**; it becomes palpable only once substantially enlarged. Because the spine, kidney and diaphragm block other directions, it grows **downwards and towards the right iliac fossa**, roughly along the line of the 10th rib.

blocks.title: Palpating the spleen
items: Start in the right iliac fossa and work towards the left upper quadrant.
Keep the hand still and ask for a deep breath, so the descending edge meets your fingers.
Use your left hand around the lower left ribs to pull the spleen forward.
For a small spleen, roll the patient onto the right side and repeat.

blocks.title: Features that identify a spleen (versus an enlarged left kidney)
items: Palpable notch on the leading edge.
Superficial and dull to percussion.
Moves well with breathing.
You cannot get your hand between the costal margin and the mass (no upper border).

blocks.title: Percussion signs
items: **Traube's space** (bounded by the 6th rib, mid-axillary line and left costal margin) is normally resonant; dullness suggests splenomegaly (or pleural effusion).
**Castell's spot**: lowest left intercostal space in the anterior axillary line; it turns dull in full inspiration if the spleen is enlarged.
Likelihood ratios (LR+): palpable spleen 8.2, Traube dullness 2.3, Castell spot 1.2. Palpation is the most useful sign.

blocks.title: Causes of splenomegaly by size
rows: CML, myelofibrosis, chronic malaria, visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar); Talley adds CLL and primary splenic lymphoma; rarely Gaucher's
The above plus portal hypertension, non-Hodgkin lymphoma, acute or chronic leukaemia, thalassaemia, storage diseases
The above plus PV, essential thrombocythaemia, haemolytic anaemia, megaloblastic anaemia (rarely), infections (infectious mononucleosis, hepatitis, endocarditis, malaria), RA, SLE, amyloid, sarcoid

blocks.text: Lists of **massive** splenomegaly differ: Davidson marks CML, myelofibrosis, malaria and kala-azar; Talley also lists CLL as a common massive cause; Kumar adds Gaucher's disease as a rare one. Use Davidson's list in exams.

blocks.title: Reading the pattern
items: **Hepatosplenomegaly**: lympho- or myeloproliferative disease, liver disease, or infiltration (e.g. amyloid).
**Splenomegaly + lymphadenopathy**: lymphoproliferative disease (e.g. CLL, lymphoma).
**Hypersplenism** (any big spleen, e.g. blood disease, portal hypertension, Felty's, lymphoma): pancytopenia, haemolysis, increased plasma volume.
**CML**: splenomegaly, often massive, is the key sign and may cause abdominal discomfort. **CLL**: often asymptomatic; otherwise infections, anaemia, painless nodes, left upper quadrant discomfort.
**ITP**: examination is normal apart from bleeding; splenomegaly is rare. **Aplastic anaemia**: nodes and hepatosplenomegaly are rare, so finding them suggests another diagnosis.

blocks.text: An MCQ answer key states the spleen is enlarged in about 20% of ITP. Kumar describes ITP as a normal examination apart from bleeding, with **splenomegaly rare**, and Davidson's ITP account does not list splenomegaly as a feature. Follow the textbooks.

blocks.title: Completing the abdomen and examination
items: Feel for hepatomegaly, ascites and masses; para-aortic nodes (a deep central mass strongly suggests lymphoma or lymphatic leukaemia); inguinal nodes; testes.
Rectal and pelvic examination for bleeding or tumour.
Finish with fundi, temperature chart and urinalysis (blood, urobilinogen).

blocks.text: Imaging (ultrasound or CT) confirms splenomegaly and also shows the liver and abdominal lymph nodes.

blocks.note: Look at: position of the Castell spot for splenic percussion

cards.front: Haematocrit level that should prompt investigation for polycythaemia?
cards.back: Persistently > 0.52 (men) or > 0.48 (women) for over 2 months; > 0.60 / > 0.56 can be assumed absolute erythrocytosis

cards.front: Itch after a hot bath, headache and plethora in a man over 60: likely diagnosis and key test?
Burning, red, warm feet with a very high platelet count?
Oval vs round macrocytes: what do they suggest?
cards.back: Oval: B12 or folate deficiency. Round: alcohol or liver disease

cards.front: Neutrophil count defining neutropenia, and the critical level?
Three symptom groups to ask about in suspected haematological malignancy?
cards.back: Marrow failure (anaemia, bleeding, infection), mass effect (spleen, nodes), systemic (fever, night sweats, weight loss)

cards.front: Pain in an enlarged node after drinking alcohol suggests?
How is performance status judged from the history, and why does it matter?
cards.back: From activities of daily living (washing, dressing, shopping, cooking); predicts tolerance of chemotherapy or stem cell transplant

cards.front: Bleeding immediately after surgery vs bleeding hours later: which defect?
cards.back: Immediate: platelet plug (primary haemostasis). Delayed: coagulation factor defect

cards.front: What fraction of haemophilia cases have no family history?

cards.back: VTE < 45 y, recurrent VTE, family history of unprovoked/recurrent clots, combined arterial + venous, unusual sites (cerebral, hepatic, portal, mesenteric)

cards.front: Raised (palpable) purpura: thrombocytopenia or something else?
cards.back: Not thrombocytopenia: suggests vasculitis or bacteraemia

cards.front: Gum hypertrophy in a pancytopenic patient suggests?
Hard left supraclavicular node with weight loss and early satiety?
Node feature with the highest LR+ for serious disease?
cards.back: Fixed node (LR+ 13); tender nodes argue against (LR+ 0.61)

cards.front: Where is the Castell spot, and what is a positive sign?
cards.back: Lowest left intercostal space, anterior axillary line; dull on full inspiration if the spleen is enlarged

questions.theme: Raised red cell or platelet counts
questions.leadIn: For each patient, choose the single most likely answer from the list. An option may fit several patients, or none at all.

items.stem: A 68-year-old non-smoker reports intense itching every time he gets out of a hot bath, plus headaches and blurred vision. He is plethoric, his spleen tip is palpable and his haematocrit is 0.59. Oxygen saturation is normal.
items.explanation: Aquagenic itch, plethora and a palpable spleen in an older patient with normal oxygen saturation fit primary polycythaemia (PV), which carries JAK2 V617F in over 90%.

items.stem: A 54-year-old overweight man with hypertension treated with a thiazide diuretic smokes 25 cigarettes a day and drinks heavily. His haematocrit is 0.53 but his red cell mass is normal and his plasma volume is reduced.
items.explanation: Raised haematocrit with a normal red cell mass and low plasma volume is apparent (relative) polycythaemia, linked to hypertension, smoking, alcohol and diuretics.

items.stem: A 59-year-old woman has episodes of severe burning pain with redness and warmth in both feet. Her haemoglobin and white count are normal, but her platelet count is 980 × 10^9/L on repeated tests, and she has no infection, inflammation or cancer.
items.explanation: Erythromelalgia with a persistently high platelet count and no reactive cause points to essential thrombocythaemia. Two steps: exclude reactive thrombocytosis (commoner) first, then recognise the classic symptom.

questions.leadIn: For each patient, choose the single most likely answer from the list. An option may fit several patients, or none at all.

items.stem: A 23-year-old man has had a painless lump in the right side of his neck for 2 months. He has noticed generalised itch, and the lump aches whenever he drinks beer. On examination the node is 3 cm and rubbery.
items.explanation: Painless rubbery cervical node in a young adult with pruritus and alcohol-induced node pain is the classic Hodgkin picture.

items.stem: A 71-year-old woman has low back pain, increasing thirst and constipation. She has had two pneumonias this year. Her bloods reveal anaemia with a raised creatinine.
items.explanation: Calcium symptoms, renal impairment, anaemia and bone pain (CRAB) plus recurrent infection point to myeloma.

items.stem: A 63-year-old man completed chemotherapy and radiotherapy for lymphoma 6 years ago and has stayed in remission. He now has fatigue and easy bruising, and his count shows pancytopenia with abnormal-looking (dysplastic) precursors.
items.explanation: Two steps: prior cytotoxic drugs and radiation are known risk factors for a new blood cancer; cytopenias with dysplasia years later fit therapy-related myelodysplasia rather than lymphoma relapse.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old man is referred after a tooth extraction. The socket stopped bleeding initially, but he began bleeding again several hours later and continued for 2 days. As a teenager he had a hot, swollen knee after a minor football tackle. His maternal grandfather was "a bleeder".
questions.leadIn: Which type of haemostatic defect is most likely?
questions.explanation: Delayed bleeding after a surgical challenge, a haemarthrosis and an X-linked family pattern (maternal grandfather) all point to a coagulation factor defect such as haemophilia.
whyNot: Low platelets cause immediate mucosal and skin bleeding, not haemarthrosis.
Platelet function defects bleed immediately after surgery and cause petechiae and mucosal bleeding.
VWD gives a mucosal (platelet-type) pattern with immediate bleeding and dominant inheritance.
A local lesion causes repeated bleeding from one site, not joint bleeding plus a family history.

questions.stem: A haematology clinic reviews referrals for possible thrombophilia testing.
questions.leadIn: Which history most clearly fits a recognised indication for testing?
options: Below-knee DVT aged 71, ten days after a knee replacement
Pulmonary embolism aged 66 during chemotherapy for pancreatic cancer
Mesenteric vein thrombosis aged 52 with no obvious trigger
Ischaemic stroke aged 74 with atrial fibrillation
DVT aged 58 after three weeks bed-bound with pneumonia
questions.explanation: Venous thrombosis at an unusual site (cerebral, hepatic, portal or mesenteric veins) is an indication; others are VTE under 45, recurrent VTE, a strong family history, and combined arterial and venous events.
whyNot: Provoked by orthopaedic surgery in an older patient; no indication.
Explained by malignancy and chemotherapy; testing adds little.
An arterial event with a clear cardioembolic cause.
Provoked by immobility and illness, and over 45.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man has a haemoglobin of 78 g/L. A student examines him to see which bedside sign best supports anaemia.
questions.leadIn: Which sign is the most reliable?
questions.explanation: Conjunctival pallor is more reliable than nail-bed or palmar pallor; when present it helps, though its absence does not exclude anaemia.
whyNot: Nail-bed pallor is an unreliable sign.
Palmar crease pallor suggests Hb below about 70 g/L but is also unreliable.
Koilonychia hints at the cause (long-standing iron deficiency) and is rarely seen.
Tachycardia is a non-specific compensatory sign with many causes.

questions.stem: A 73-year-old man with a large IgM paraprotein (macroglobulinaemia) becomes intermittently confused and complains of blurred vision.
questions.leadIn: What is fundoscopy most likely to show?
questions.explanation: Hyperviscosity (macroglobulinaemia, myeloproliferative disease, CML) causes engorged retinal veins, haemorrhages and later papilloedema; fluctuating consciousness is another hyperviscosity feature.
whyNot: Yellow-white patches suggest toxoplasma or CMV retinitis.
Optic atrophy is a feature of B12 deficiency.
Isolated haemorrhages fit thrombocytopenia; hyperviscosity also distends veins.
With symptomatic hyperviscosity the veins are expected to be engorged.

questions.leadIn: For each patient, choose the single most likely answer from the list. An option may fit several patients, or none at all.

items.stem: A 67-year-old man has lost 9 kg and feels full after a few mouthfuls. A hard, 2 cm node is felt in the left supraclavicular fossa.
items.explanation: A hard left supraclavicular node with weight loss and early satiety is Troisier's sign of gastric cancer.

items.stem: A 19-year-old student has fever, a very sore throat and tender cervical nodes. A widespread rash appeared after she was given ampicillin.
items.explanation: Fever, sore throat, lymphadenopathy and an ampicillin rash are the keyword cluster for infectious mononucleosis.

items.stem: A 46-year-old woman has a hard axillary node that is fixed to deep tissue on the left. The overlying skin is not inflamed.
items.explanation: Hard, fixed axillary nodes suggest carcinoma; the breast is the drainage area to examine.

items.stem: A 52-year-old man has enlarged epitrochlear nodes on both sides, painless rubbery nodes in both axillae and groins, and night sweats. He has no skin wounds on his arms.
items.explanation: Two steps: an enlarged epitrochlear node without arm infection is usually pathological; with generalised painless rubbery nodes and B symptoms, non-Hodgkin lymphoma fits best (Hodgkin tends to be localised).

questions.leadIn: For each patient, choose the single most likely answer from the list. An option may fit several patients, or none at all.

items.stem: A 47-year-old man has early satiety and a spleen reaching the right iliac fossa. White count is 190 × 10^9/L with a raised basophil count.
items.explanation: Massive splenomegaly with a very high white count and raised basophils is chronic myeloid leukaemia; splenomegaly, often massive, is its key physical sign.

items.stem: A 61-year-old woman who has had rheumatoid arthritis for many years has recurrent infections and leg ulcers. Her spleen is palpable and her neutrophil count is 0.8 × 10^9/L.
items.explanation: Rheumatoid arthritis plus splenomegaly plus neutropenia defines Felty's syndrome, which can also cause leg ulcers.

items.stem: A 50-year-old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis has ascites and a moderately enlarged spleen. His platelets and white cells are both mildly low.
items.explanation: Two steps: cirrhosis causes congestive splenomegaly through portal hypertension, and the big spleen then causes hypersplenism (cytopenias).

items.stem: A 35-year-old farmer from an endemic rural region has months of fever and weight loss. His spleen is massive and he is pancytopenic.
items.explanation: Massive splenomegaly with fever and weight loss in someone from an endemic area suggests kala-azar, one of Davidson's massive causes.

questions.leadIn: For each patient, choose the single most likely answer from the list. An option may fit several patients, or none at all.

items.stem: An 8-year-old boy has a hot, swollen knee after a minor fall and a large thigh haematoma after an injection. His mother's brother had similar problems.
items.explanation: Joint and deep muscle bleeding in a boy with an affected maternal uncle is an X-linked coagulation factor deficiency.

items.stem: A 21-year-old woman has had heavy periods since her first period and frequent nosebleeds. She bled straight away and for hours after a wisdom tooth extraction. Her father bruises easily. Platelet count, PT and APTT are normal.
items.explanation: Mucosal, immediate bleeding with an autosomal (father-to-daughter) pattern and normal screening tests is typical of von Willebrand disease; screens can miss it.

items.stem: A 74-year-old widower who lives on tea and toast has swollen, bleeding gums and tiny bleeds around the hair follicles on his shins.
items.explanation: Perifollicular purpura on the legs is almost diagnostic of scurvy, with swollen gums supporting it.

items.stem: A 7-year-old girl has raised purpuric spots over her buttocks and the backs of her legs, colicky abdominal pain, sore ankles and blood in her urine. Her platelet count is normal.
items.explanation: Palpable purpura is a vasculitic, not thrombocytopenic, sign; with abdominal pain, arthralgia and nephritis it is Henoch–Schönlein purpura.

items.stem: A 55-year-old man has recurrent nosebleeds and iron deficiency anaemia. Several tiny red vascular spots are visible on his lips and tongue.
items.explanation: Telangiectasia of lips and tongue with recurrent bleeding indicates hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman has drenching night sweats that soak her nightclothes, has lost 8 kg in 3 months and has painless, rubbery nodes in both axillae. FBC, ESR and chest X-ray have been done.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate investigation to establish the diagnosis?
options: Excision biopsy of a representative node
questions.explanation: Suspected lymphoma must be confirmed histologically on a representative node biopsy large enough for histology, immunology and molecular studies.
whyNot: FNA does not give enough tissue to classify lymphoma.
Marrow may be involved but is not the diagnostic test of choice.
A film may be normal in nodal lymphoma.
Waiting delays diagnosis when B symptoms suggest malignancy.

questions.stem: A student examining a 50-year-old with an enlarged neck node wants to know which finding most increases the likelihood of serious disease such as lymphoma.
questions.leadIn: Which finding has the highest positive likelihood ratio?
questions.explanation: A fixed node has an LR+ of about 13, well above size over 9 cm² (8.4), hard texture (3.3), supraclavicular site (3.1) and age over 40 (2.25).
whyNot: Tenderness lowers the probability (LR+ 0.61) and suggests infection.
Supraclavicular site is useful but weaker (LR+ 3.1).
Hard texture has LR+ 3.3.
Age over 40 has LR+ 2.25.

questions.stem: A mass is felt in the left upper quadrant of a 64-year-old man with a high white count.
questions.leadIn: Which finding best indicates that the mass is the spleen?
options: The examining hand cannot be placed between the mass and the costal margin
The note over the mass is resonant
The mass does not move with respiration
The mass has a smooth edge with no notch
The mass enlarges towards the left loin
questions.explanation: You cannot get above a spleen. It is also superficial, dull, notched and moves well with breathing, and it grows towards the right iliac fossa.
whyNot: The spleen is dull to percussion.
The spleen moves well with respiration.
A notch on the leading edge supports a spleen.
An enlarging spleen grows down and towards the right iliac fossa.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old woman has a macrocytic anaemia with low vitamin B12. She had an operation many years ago that removed the source of intrinsic factor.
questions.leadIn: Which operation is the most likely?
questions.explanation: Gastric resection removes intrinsic factor production; terminal ileal resection also causes B12 deficiency, but by removing the absorption site, not intrinsic factor.
whyNot: Ileal resection causes B12 malabsorption but intrinsic factor is still made.
Gallbladder removal does not affect B12.
The colon is not involved in B12 absorption.
Splenectomy does not cause B12 deficiency.

questions.leadIn: For each patient, choose the physical sign you would most expect to find. An option may fit several patients, or none at all.

items.stem: A 45-year-old man has fever, fatigue and bruising. His count shows pancytopenia with blasts that have monocytic features.
items.explanation: Step 1: pancytopenia with blasts means acute leukaemia. Step 2: monocytic AML infiltrates the gums. So expect gum hypertrophy; check the mouth for ulcers and bleeding too.

items.stem: A 66-year-old woman has back pain, hypercalcaemia and renal impairment, and an IgG paraprotein is found.
items.explanation: Step 1: CRAB features plus a paraprotein mean myeloma. Step 2: myeloma expands the marrow, so tapping the spine or pressing the sternum is tender.

items.stem: A 20-year-old man with sickle cell disease has had a slowly healing sore on his lower leg for months.
items.explanation: Step 1: sickle cell disease is a haemolytic anaemia. Step 2: abnormal blood viscosity causes tissue infarction, giving ulcers just above the medial or lateral malleolus.

questions.leadIn: For each patient, choose the drug most likely to be responsible. An option may fit several patients, or none at all.

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman started treatment for Graves' disease 6 weeks ago. She now has fever and a sore throat; neutrophils are 0.2 × 10^9/L.
items.explanation: Antithyroid drugs (carbimazole, propylthiouracil) are classic causes of severe neutropenia; fever may be the only sign of infection.

items.stem: A 40-year-old man developed jaundice and dark urine a few days after starting an antibiotic for a urinary infection. His haemoglobin has fallen.
items.explanation: Sulphonamides are listed as a drug cause of haemolysis in the anaemia drug history.

items.stem: A 66-year-old woman on day 7 after hip surgery, receiving injections to prevent clots, has a 50% fall in platelet count and a new DVT.
items.explanation: Heparin is a recognised drug cause of thrombocytopenia; heparin-induced thrombocytopenia with thrombosis is also a haematological cause of clotting.

items.stem: A 29-year-old man on long-term treatment for epilepsy has generalised enlarged lymph nodes. Infection screens and biopsy show no lymphoma.
items.explanation: Two steps: generalised nodes have a short drug list; in an epileptic patient phenytoin causes a pseudolymphoma.

questions.leadIn: For each patient, choose the single most likely answer from the list. An option may fit several patients, or none at all.

items.stem: A 23-year-old woman develops a DVT 3 months after starting the combined contraceptive pill. Her mother and brother both had unprovoked DVTs.
items.explanation: Two steps: a strong family history suggests an inherited thrombophilia; factor V Leiden interacts with the pill, raising risk about 100-fold.

items.stem: A 41-year-old woman with SLE has had a DVT and, this year, a stroke.
items.explanation: Combined arterial and venous thrombosis in a patient with SLE points to antiphospholipid syndrome.

items.stem: A 63-year-old man has hepatic vein thrombosis. He is plethoric with a palpable spleen and his haematocrit is 0.61.
items.explanation: Thrombosis at an unusual site with a high haematocrit and splenomegaly suggests polycythaemia vera (test JAK2).

items.stem: A 67-year-old former smoker has an unprovoked DVT. He mentions he has lost 7 kg without trying over the last 4 months.
items.explanation: Unprovoked VTE with unexplained weight loss raises suspicion of malignancy, a major medical thrombosis risk factor.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman with immune thrombocytopenia asks when she is likely to start bleeding spontaneously.
questions.leadIn: Below which platelet count (× 10^9/L) does spontaneous bleeding usually start, if platelet function is normal?
questions.explanation: Spontaneous bleeding is unusual until the count drops below about 20 × 10^9/L; below 10 × 10^9/L retinal and intracranial bleeding can occur.
whyNot: 150 is around the lower limit of normal; no bleeding risk.
Petechiae may appear in thrombocytopenia below about 100, but spontaneous bleeding is unusual at this level.
Counts around 50 seldom bleed without trauma or surgery.
Below 10 is the level for retinal and intracranial bleeding, not the usual start of spontaneous bleeding.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old man has newly diagnosed acute myeloid leukaemia. The team needs to decide whether intensive chemotherapy is appropriate.
questions.leadIn: Which part of the history most directly helps assess his performance status?
options: Whether he can wash, dress, shop and cook independently
The ages and health of his siblings
How long his night sweats have lasted
questions.explanation: Performance status is judged from activities of daily living and predicts tolerance of chemotherapy or stem cell transplantation.
whyNot: Sibling details matter for donor selection, not performance status.
Benzene is a risk factor for the disease, not a fitness measure.
Sweats describe the disease, not his fitness.
Family history explores risk, not fitness.

questions.theme: Recurrent infection and white cell disorders
questions.leadIn: For each patient, choose the single most likely answer from the list. An option may fit several patients, or none at all.

items.stem: A 30-year-old man has had recurrent sinusitis and chest infections since childhood and now has a chronic productive cough from bronchiectasis. His full blood count is normal.
items.explanation: Recurrent sinus and respiratory infections leading to bronchiectasis, with a normal count, suggest an antibody (immunoglobulin) deficiency.

items.stem: A 76-year-old man has a raised lymphocyte count found on routine bloods, small painless nodes in the neck and axillae, and two chest infections this winter.
items.explanation: An older patient with lymphocytosis, painless generalised nodes and infections fits CLL, often found incidentally.

items.stem: A 24-year-old woman has bruising, petechiae and recurrent mouth infections. Her count shows pancytopenia with almost no reticulocytes, and the film shows no blasts or other abnormal cells. There is no lymphadenopathy, and neither liver nor spleen is palpable.
items.explanation: Two steps: pancytopenia means marrow failure or infiltration; no blasts on the film argues against acute leukaemia, and absent reticulocytes with no nodes or hepatosplenomegaly fit aplastic anaemia, in which nodes and organomegaly are rare.

questions.stem: An 18-year-old woman has heavy periods, frequent nosebleeds and bled straight away after a tonsillectomy. Her father has similar problems. Platelet count, PT and APTT are normal.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Measure von Willebrand factor and platelet function
Reassure her, as normal screens exclude a bleeding disorder
questions.explanation: A strong bleeding history with normal screening tests calls for VWF and platelet function testing; screens miss von Willebrand disease.
whyNot: There is no evidence of marrow disease; the count is normal.
Haemophilia B gives a coagulation pattern (joints, muscles, delayed bleeding) in males.
Screening tests do not reliably detect all bleeding disorders.
Thrombophilia testing is for clotting, not bleeding.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man has had headaches and itching after hot baths for a year. He is plethoric with a palpable spleen. Haematocrit is 0.61 and oxygen saturation is 98% on air. He does not smoke.
questions.leadIn: Which investigation is most useful next?
questions.explanation: Aquagenic itch, plethora and splenomegaly with normal oxygenation suggest primary polycythaemia; JAK2 V617F is present in over 90% of PV.
whyNot: BCR-ABL is for suspected CML, which presents with a very high white count rather than a raised haematocrit.
Electrophoresis looks for haemoglobinopathies, not polycythaemia.
Normal saturation and no smoking or lung disease make hypoxic secondary polycythaemia unlikely.
B12 levels do not establish the cause of polycythaemia.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old woman has anaemia and hypercalcaemia. When the examiner taps over her spine and presses on her sternum she winces.
questions.leadIn: Which diagnosis does this sign most support?
questions.explanation: Bony tenderness reflects marrow expansion by myeloma, lymphoma or carcinoma; anaemia and high calcium fit myeloma (CRAB).
whyNot: ITP causes bleeding signs only; examination is otherwise normal.
Iron deficiency does not expand the marrow or raise calcium.
Spherocytosis causes jaundice and splenomegaly, not bone tenderness with hypercalcaemia.
PV causes plethora and splenomegaly, not anaemia.

ospe.identify: Petechial purpura: flat, pinpoint, non-blanching bleeds into the dermis, seen with thrombocytopenia or platelet dysfunction
Ecchymoses: bruises larger than 5 mm (contrast with the pinhead petechiae of Fig. 21.4)
Polycythaemia vera: prominent, injected scleral blood vessels (conjunctival suffusion)
Henoch–Schönlein purpura: palpable purpura on the legs; a vasculitic, not thrombocytopenic, rash
Gum hypertrophy from leukaemic infiltration in acute myeloid leukaemia (inset); also koilonychia and angular stomatitis of iron deficiency
Cervical and submandibular lymphadenopathy; name the eight cervical/supraclavicular node groups on the diagram
